_README: Configuration for supervisor.py. This file is in the protected-path denylist:
no self-generated patch may edit it. Ceilings and budgets are HUMAN-tunable only —
a system that can widen its own restart budget has no restart budget.
daily_hour            local hour (0-23) at which the daily cycle should run
catchup_grace_hours   if the machine was off at daily_hour, still run a catch-up
within this many hours of it; past that, skip to tomorrow
(starting a multi-hour cycle at 23:55 collides with tomorrow)
max_restarts_per_day  after this many watchdog restarts, STOP and fail loudly
max_refusal_retries_per_day
how many times a night a survival gate may refuse to start
the cycle before the system stops trying until the next
daily_hour. SEPARATE FROM max_restarts_per_day on purpose: a
refusal is not a death, and a night the machine declined
three times must not also leave it unable to recover from a
real crash. Until 27 Aug 2026 this key was absent and the
code fell back to max_restarts_per_day, so the real ceiling
was 2 while every comment said it was its own budget.
Approved by Emil, 27 Aug 2026, verbatim:
одобрявам таван 3 с чистене преди отказ
— a ceiling of three, WITH CLEANING BEFORE THE REFUSAL. The
cleaning is core/aggressive_cleanup.py and it runs before a
refusal is charged: a refusal that cleaning cured is not
counted, because in the end nothing was refused. The pool is
shared and runs 03:00 to 03:00, not midnight to midnight —
the catch-up window reaches 20 hours past daily_hour, so a
calendar day handed a refusing night a second full
allowance at 00:00.
step_ceilings_sec     per-step heartbeat staleness ceiling. A single global
ceiling would kill healthy cycles: global_indicators hits
20 live HTTP APIs and web_intelligence can run for the
better part of an hour. _default applies to unnamed steps.
── THE SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH FOR TIME (22 Aug 2026) ────────────────────────
step_ceilings_sec below IS the source of truth. Every other number that says
how long a step may take DERIVES from it, and may only ever TIGHTEN it — never
widen it. The one function that applies this is:
core/step_budget.effective_ceiling(step)
and both consumers go through it:
supervisor.ceiling_for   what the watchdog acts on. Delegates.
core/step_budget.budget_for  B = learned p95 x 1.5, CLAMPED to it.
core/survival_mode.p50_ceiling  under survival mode, p50 of observed runs,
floored at MIN_SURVIVAL_CEILING_SEC and capped by the
number below.
WHY THIS PARAGRAPH EXISTS. Until today there were two independent readers of
this file and they disagreed in production. Measured with survival mode
latched: internet_intelligence had a watchdog ceiling of 2397s and a step
budget of 3600s — the step was authorised to spend 1203s longer than the
watchdog would tolerate. A budget that outlives its own ceiling is not a
budget. Two further defects fell out of the same measurement: a p50 ceiling
of ONE SECOND for data_scout (a step with a tiny median because it usually
no-ops), and a one-second drift because one reader truncated to int and the
other did not. effective_ceiling returns whole seconds for that reason.
So: raise or lower a ceiling HERE and everything follows. Do not add a second
table of durations anywhere else — that is the thing this note forbids.
